Caveat: this is one 30-day window, so confirm the 25% holds and isn't a tracking gap between Meesho's checkout and your purchase event. But a leak this large at the last step is real money, and it's the highest-leverage thing you can fix.

an0567.user: Skincare brand, running Amazon Ads, spent ₹19.5L last month and this is post-iOS so attribution is a mess. The platform dashboard says my ROAS is 4.0, but my Shopify last-click report says 1.5 for the same period. They don't match at all and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. Which do I trust?
an0567.assistant:
Neither, exactly — and that's the answer, not a dodge. Both numbers are biased in opposite directions, and the truth sits somewhere in the middle.

The platform's 4.0 is generous on purpose: it uses modelled conversions and a 7-day-click (often view-through) window, so it claims credit for sales that would've happened anyway and for people who saw an ad but bought via another route. Shopify last-click's 1.5 is the opposite — it only credits the very last touch, so it hands all the glory to Google-brand-search or direct traffic and undercounts the ads that did the early convincing. One over-claims, one under-claims. They will never agree, and refereeing them every month is a waste of your energy.

Stop trying to pick a winner between two dashboards. Anchor on the one number neither can spin: blended CAC. Take total spend across everything ÷ actual new customers Shopify recorded that month. On ₹19.5L, if you brought in, say, 1,000 genuinely new customers, that's ₹1,950 all-in CAC — a real, conservative number you can compare against your contribution per customer and manage to.

Manage to blended CAC and contribution, not platform ROAS. Caveat: blended CAC blurs which specific channel did the work — for that you'd run a proper holdout or geo-test later. But for deciding whether you're profitable overall, it's the honest number, and it cuts through this exact mess.
